weighing-animal-minds-part-ii.html:
If the "numbers" reach conclusions that clash with moral intuitions, something is deeply wrong with the numbers, because we aren't discussing about physical systems.

Suffering and pain are hard to quantify when we have no access to exactly what any of those state are. Between humans we can make some inferences from brain structures and behaviors. With mammals we can extend it. But with shrimps?

I find it far more respectable to simply recommend/advocate for vegetarianism or veganism, which resolves the moral calculus, instead of a dubious ordering of animals moral weight. Because once you start ordering other animals, why stop there and not include people and their different levels of cognitive abilities?

This was a great post! Thanks for the plug.

> Technically you can “count clicks”. The dial clicks as you rotate it; a full dose is 60 clicks, so 30 clicks gives you half a dose, 15 a quarter, etc. But the pen will only deliver four doses regardless of size and then it locks you out!

Eh??? That has not been my experience at all. My Kwikpen lets me dispense any dose, arbitrarily many times. It eventually locks me out, but only once I hit the total number of clicks in the pen. E.g. the last pen that I finished (nominally 4x15mg = 60mg, 240 clicks total) lasted 257 clicks according to my spreadsheet. When it locked, there was still about a quarter of the serum left in the pen, based on the markings on the side. But I still discarded it because it had lasted me ~4 months, and it was time for a new one.

However, my Kwikpen is from Canada. Maybe the four-dose lockout is a UK thing? Did this actually happen to you, or did someone tell you it happens?

the-median-take-is-taken.name: Cabeza de Vaca
the-median-take-is-taken.html:
I sort of agree with this but...

I can easily imagine a near-future world where Claude is very good at noticing odd mental gaps/unasked questions ("Claude, find me 10 surprisingly unasked questions concerning XYZ topics you think I'll like from what you know of me"), and likewise one where Claude names patterns.

The moral urgency point is interesting: could you imagine a world where Claude pesters you in the same way your Vegan friends do? Maybe so: I have seen Claude morally chide users before. And maybe Claude will do it more persuasively in the style of, say, David Foster Wallace?

I remain committed to my narrower criteria for long-lasting writing, https://alec.freumh.org/WTP.html

Then again, maybe we are in a very important interstitial time in which persuading people/influencing discourse does have an effect today, but where you constantly have to adapt to achieve influence. I can see why you might push the needle of discourse today (using your three tricks above, which work at the moment) on the assumption that if you can persuade a few people then their brain-states might determine the future of the universe.

Otherwise, this aside, I think this might simply be a case of a more refined case of blogs-as-anecdotes. E.g., that guy in the friends' group who coins all the nicknames and cool phrases, or pesters us about our moral integrity.

the-median-take-is-taken.name: Henry Stanley
the-median-take-is-taken.html:
> could you imagine a world where Claude pesters you in the same way your Vegan friends do? Maybe so: I have seen Claude morally chide users before.

I think this is very unlikely given LLMs are trained to be helpful assistants. Users don't want their to be told to go vegan! Especially so if model makers are doing RL on the feedback that users are giving them (ie users upvoting/downvoting replies). This behaviour would just be trained out.

Perhaps once Anthropic becomes the de facto world government, maybe

> I can easily imagine a near-future world where Claude is very good at noticing odd mental gaps/unasked questions

I agree that this seems more plausible, and LLMs can probably pushed into this sort of behaviour by careful prompting

> Otherwise, this aside, I think this might simply be a case of a more refined case of blogs-as-anecdotes.

I think we're in agreement on that. I doubt any of our work will persist through 'deep time' – but I'd settle if something I wrote was still being cited in a few years (rather than just disappearing in a pile of turboslop as most of it surely will)

should-anyone-be-vegan.name: Catherine Kelaher
should-anyone-be-vegan.html:
This was a great read.

The abolitionist analogy is the strongest part of this piece for me, and I think it deserves to be taken further. We wouldn’t say an abolitionist who kept slaves was doing their best simply because they also donated to the cause. Personal participation in harm doesn’t become neutral just because it’s offset elsewhere.

I think you’re right that effectiveness arguments are worth having, and that donations can do enormous good. But they don’t really resolve the question of what you’re doing with your own hands, your own money, your own plate. Veganism isn’t a lifestyle add-on. It’s just the minimum coherent position if you believe animals shouldn’t suffer for our convenience.

Funding opposition to any form of violence whilst also personally sustaining it isn’t neutral. It’s a contradiction worth sitting with.

my-claude-code-workflow.name: David Mears
my-claude-code-workflow.html:
Because I'm employed by a workplace and don't want to pay my own money, and my workplace is on Microsoft, I'm trying out using Claude Opus 4.5 as an agent via the GitHub Copilot feature (also accessible with GitHub CLI). I'll (maybe) let you know how it goes! I'm hoping it will give me more parallelisability of agents than an IDE-based agent. I'm already benefitting from your 'worktree' tip since I hadn't actually come across that git feature till now - much better for context-switching mid-flow.

So far my impression is that this way of using Claude might require less handholding than you allude to -- I don't have to tell it to 'do it yourself'. I guess the scaffolding is pretty decent. But nor have I yet tested it with a really meaty feature.

I wonder if my main blocker to using AI agents going forward might be getting co-workers on board: there are some norms to establish like how to trust that the human co-author has actually thoroughly reviewed what the agent has written (and is not just fobbing off that detail-oriented work to the second human reviewer). Also, I don't like when my coworkers use AI-generated commit messages (generated by an AI other than the actual agent who wrote the code, i.e. the dumb bot that lives in the GitLens VSCode extension) - needless to say, those are not very correlated with the actual reasons for the changes.

I will be referring to your blog post and Boris from Claude Code's twitter thread: https://x.com/bcherny/status/2007179832300581177?s=20
